rows.stem: The momentum of a photon is \(5.0 \times 10^{-29}\) kg. m/s. Ignoring relativistic effects (if any), the wavelength of the photon is
rows.context:
When a photon of suitable frequency is incident on a metal surface, photoelectron is emitted from it. If the frequency is below a threshold frequency \((
u_0)\) for the surface, no photoelectron is emitted. For a photon of frequency \(
u(
u > 
u_0)\), the kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is \(h(
u - 
u_0)\). The photocurrent can be stopped by applying a potential \(V_0\) called 'stopping potential' on the anode. Thus maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons \(K_m = eV_0 = h(
u - 
u_0)\). The experimental graph between \(V_0\) and \(
u\) for a metal is shown in figure. This is a straight line of slope m.
rows.solution:
A photon's momentum and wavelength are related by the de Broglie relation, which for a photon follows directly from \(E = pc\) and \(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\):
\(p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\)
Substituting \(h = 6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}\) and \(p = 5{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-29}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\):
\(\lambda = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}}{5{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-29}}\)
\(\lambda = 1{\cdot}326 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m}\)
Converting to micrometres, with \(1\ \mu\mathrm{m} = 10^{-6}\) m:
\(\lambda \approx 13{\cdot}3\ \mu\mathrm{m}\)
The wavelength is about \(13{\cdot}3\ \mu\mathrm{m}\), which places this photon in the infrared.
The distractor \(1{\cdot}33\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) differs by exactly a factor of ten, which is what an error in the power of ten produces; \(3{\cdot}3\) and \(16{\cdot}6\) come from mishandling the leading digits. Since the arithmetic is a single division, the safeguard is to carry the exponents separately: \(10^{-34}\) divided by \(10^{-29}\) is \(10^{-5}\), and \(\dfrac{6{\cdot}63}{5{\cdot}0} = 1{\cdot}326\).
The instruction to ignore relativistic effects is a courtesy rather than a necessity here: \(p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}\) is exact for a photon, which is always relativistic and always massless.

rows.subtopic: Electrostatic Potential due to Charges and Dipoles
rows.stem:
(i) A small conducting sphere A of radius r charged to a potential V, is enclosed by a spherical conducting shell B of radius R. If A and B are connected by a thin wire, calculate the final potential on sphere A and shell B.
(ii) Write two characteristics of equipotential surfaces. A uniform electric field of 50 NC\(^{-1}\) is set up in a region along \(+x\) axis. If the potential at the origin (0, 0) is 220 V, find the potential at a point (4m, 3m).
rows.solution:
(i) THE SPHERE AND SHELL CONNECTED BY A WIRE.
Sphere A of radius r is charged to potential V, so its charge is
\(V = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q = 4\pi\varepsilon_{0}rV\)
When A and B are joined by a wire, they become ONE conductor, and charge flows until the whole conductor is at a single potential. The essential point is where the charge goes: on a conductor, charge resides entirely on the OUTER surface, so ALL of A's charge flows out to the shell B. Sphere A is left with none.
POTENTIAL ON SHELL B, now carrying the whole charge Q on its radius R:
\(V_{B} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{Q}{R} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} \times \dfrac{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}rV}{R}\)
\(V_{B} = \dfrac{rV}{R}\)
POTENTIAL ON SPHERE A. Sphere A is inside the shell and connected to it, so it sits at the SAME potential:
\(V_{A} = V_{B} = \dfrac{rV}{R}\)
Both end at \(\dfrac{rV}{R}\). Since \(R > r\), this is LESS than the original V — spreading the same charge over a larger surface lowers the potential.
Note that the charge transfers COMPLETELY, however small the potential difference driving it, and regardless of which conductor was charged first. That is the principle of the Van de Graaff generator: charge sprayed onto an inner electrode is carried entirely to the outer sphere, so charge can be added indefinitely without ever fighting the accumulated potential of the inner one.
(ii) EQUIPOTENTIAL SURFACES, AND A POTENTIAL IN A UNIFORM FIELD.
TWO CHARACTERISTICS (any two):
The potential is the SAME at every point on the surface, so NO WORK is done in moving a charge anywhere on it.
An equipotential surface is always PERPENDICULAR to the electric field lines. (If it were not, the field would have a component along the surface and moving a charge along it would require work.)
Two equipotential surfaces can never INTERSECT, since a point of intersection would have two different potentials.
FINDING THE POTENTIAL AT (4m, 3m). The field is uniform, of magnitude \(50\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\), directed along \(+x\). So the potential falls as x increases, and depends on x ALONE — the y-coordinate is irrelevant, because moving along y is moving along an equipotential.
\(V_{origin} - V = E\,\Delta x = 50 \times 4 = 200\ \mathrm{V}\)
\(V = 220 - 200\)
\(V = 20\ \mathrm{V}\)
The potential at (4m, 3m) is 20 V. The 3 m of displacement along y contributes nothing at all, which is exactly what the second characteristic above asserts.

rows.stem:
(i) What is difference between an open surface and a closed surface ? Draw elementary surface vector \(d\vec{S}\) for a spherical surface S.
(ii) Define electric flux through a surface. Give the significance of a Gaussian surface. A charge outside a Gaussian surface does not contribute to total electric flux through the surface. Why ?
(iii) A small spherical shell \(S_1\) has point charges \(q_1 = -3\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), \(q_2 = -2\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) and \(q_3 = 9\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) inside it. This shell is enclosed by another big spherical shell \(S_2\). A point charge Q is placed in between the two surfaces \(S_1\) and \(S_2\). If the electric flux through the surface \(S_2\) is four times the flux through surface \(S_1\), find charge Q.
rows.solution:
(i) OPEN AND CLOSED SURFACES.
An OPEN surface is one that does NOT enclose a volume — a sheet of paper, a hemisphere, a disc. It has a boundary edge, and it divides no region of space into an inside and an outside.
A CLOSED surface DOES enclose a volume — a complete sphere, a cube, a closed cylinder. It has no boundary edge, and it separates space into an interior and an exterior.
The distinction matters because Gauss's law applies only to CLOSED surfaces: only for those is "the charge enclosed" a meaningful quantity.
THE ELEMENTARY SURFACE VECTOR. Draw a sphere S and mark a small patch on it. Draw \(d\vec{S}\) as an arrow at that patch, PERPENDICULAR to the surface and pointing OUTWARDS, its length representing the patch's area. For a closed surface the outward normal is the agreed convention, which is what makes an outward flux positive.
(ii) ELECTRIC FLUX, THE GAUSSIAN SURFACE, AND OUTSIDE CHARGES.
DEFINITION. Electric flux through a surface is the surface integral of the field over it,
\(\phi_{E} = \oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{S} = \oint E\,dS\cos\theta\)
that is, a measure of the number of field lines crossing the surface normally.
SIGNIFICANCE OF A GAUSSIAN SURFACE. It is an imaginary closed surface chosen to exploit the SYMMETRY of a charge distribution. Chosen well, E is constant in magnitude over it and everywhere parallel to \(d\vec{S}\), so the integral collapses to \(E \times (\text{area})\) and the field can be found in one line — for a sphere, a line charge or a sheet — where direct integration would be laborious.
WHY AN OUTSIDE CHARGE CONTRIBUTES NOTHING. Every field line from a charge OUTSIDE the surface that enters it must also LEAVE it, since the line can only terminate on a charge, and there is no such charge inside. Each line therefore contributes a negative flux where it enters and an equal positive flux where it exits, and the two cancel exactly. The NET flux from any external charge is zero.
Note carefully what this does and does not say. The external charge contributes nothing to the FLUX, but it certainly contributes to the FIELD at each point of the surface. Gauss's law constrains the integral, not the integrand.
(iii) FINDING THE CHARGE Q.
Charge enclosed by the inner shell \(S_{1}\):
\(q_{1} + q_{2} + q_{3} = (-3) + (-2) + 9 = 4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)
Charge enclosed by the outer shell \(S_{2}\) — everything inside \(S_{1}\), plus Q:
\(Q + 4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)
Given that the flux through \(S_{2}\) is four times that through \(S_{1}\), and that flux is proportional to enclosed charge:
\(\dfrac{Q + 4\ \mu\mathrm{C}}{\varepsilon_{0}} = 4\left(\dfrac{4\ \mu\mathrm{C}}{\varepsilon_{0}}\right)\)
\(Q + 4 = 16\)
\(Q = 12\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)

rows.stem:
(i) What is the source of force acting on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field ? Obtain the expression for force acting between two long straight parallel conductors carrying steady currents and hence define 'ampere'.
(ii) A point charge q is moving with velocity \(\vec{v}\) in a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\). Find the work done by the magnetic force on the charge.
(iii) Explain the necessary conditions in which the trajectory of a charged particle is helical in a uniform magnetic field.
rows.solution:
(i) THE SOURCE OF THE FORCE, THE EXPRESSION, AND THE AMPERE.
THE SOURCE. A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field of its own. The force arises from the INTERACTION between that field and the external field in which the conductor is placed — equivalently, from the magnetic force \(q\vec{v} \times \vec{B}\) on each of the moving charges making up the current, summed over the conductor.
FORCE BETWEEN TWO PARALLEL CONDUCTORS. Let two long straight conductors a and b lie parallel, a distance d apart, carrying currents \(I_{a}\) and \(I_{b}\).
Conductor a produces at the position of b a field
\(B_{a} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I_{a}}{2\pi d}\)
directed perpendicular to b. A length L of conductor b, carrying \(I_{b}\) in that field, experiences
\(F_{ba} = I_{b}LB_{a} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I_{a}I_{b}}{2\pi d}L\)
so the force PER UNIT LENGTH is
\(\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I_{a}I_{b}}{2\pi d}\)
It is ATTRACTIVE when the currents are parallel and REPULSIVE when they are antiparallel. By Newton's third law conductor b exerts an equal and opposite force on a.
DEFINITION OF THE AMPERE. The ampere is that steady current which, maintained in each of two very long straight parallel conductors of negligible cross-section placed ONE METRE apart in vacuum, produces on each a force of \(2 \times 10^{-7}\) newton per metre of length.
(Substituting \(I_{a} = I_{b} = 1\) A and \(d = 1\) m into the formula gives exactly \(\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{2\pi} = 2 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\), which is where the number comes from.)
(ii) WORK DONE BY THE MAGNETIC FORCE.
The work done is ZERO.
The magnetic force is \(\vec{F} = q\left(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}\right)\), and a cross product is perpendicular to both its factors — in particular to \(\vec{v}\). The work done in a displacement \(d\vec{l} = \vec{v}\,dt\) is
\(dW = \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{l} = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}\,dt = 0\)
since \(\vec{F} \perp \vec{v}\) always.
So a magnetic field can change the DIRECTION of a charged particle's motion but never its SPEED, and hence never its kinetic energy. That is why a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field moves on a circle at constant speed, and why the cyclotron needs an ELECTRIC field to do the accelerating.
(iii) CONDITIONS FOR A HELICAL TRAJECTORY.
The path is helical when the velocity is at an ARBITRARY angle \(\theta\) to the field, with \(\theta\) neither \(0^{\circ}\) nor \(90^{\circ}\).
Resolve \(\vec{v}\) into two components. The component PERPENDICULAR to \(\vec{B}\), \(v\sin\theta\), feels the magnetic force and drives circular motion of radius \(r = \dfrac{mv\sin\theta}{qB}\). The component PARALLEL to \(\vec{B}\), \(v\cos\theta\), feels NO force, since \(\vec{v}_{\parallel} \times \vec{B} = 0\), and so continues unchanged.
A uniform circular motion superposed on a uniform straight-line drift along the axis is a HELIX. Its pitch — the distance advanced in one revolution — is
\(p = v\cos\theta \times T = \dfrac{2\pi m v\cos\theta}{qB}\)
The two special cases are the limits of this: at \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\) the parallel component vanishes and the helix closes into a CIRCLE; at \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\) the perpendicular component vanishes, no force acts at all, and the path is a STRAIGHT LINE.

rows.subtopic: Torque on a Current Loop and Magnetic Dipole
rows.stem:
(i) A current carrying loop can be considered as a magnetic dipole placed along its axis. Explain.
(ii) Obtain the relation for magnetic dipole moment \(\vec{M}\) of current carrying coil. Give the direction of \(\vec{M}\).
(iii) A current carrying coil is placed in an external uniform magnetic field. The coil is free to turn in the magnetic field. What is the net force acting on the coil ? Obtain the orientation of the coil in stable equilibrium. Show that in this orientation the flux of the total field (field produced by the loop + external field) through the coil is maximum.
rows.solution:
(i) WHY A CURRENT LOOP IS A MAGNETIC DIPOLE.
The field of a current loop, seen from a distance large compared with its size, is identical in form to that of a short bar magnet: on the axis it falls as \(\dfrac{1}{r^{3}}\) and has the value \(\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{2M}{r^{3}}\), exactly the axial field of a dipole of moment M.
The two FACES of the loop behave like the two poles. Field lines emerge from one face and enter the other, so that face acts as a NORTH pole and the other as a SOUTH pole — which face is which is given by the right-hand rule, or equivalently by whether the current appears anticlockwise or clockwise when viewed from that side.
Since the poles lie on the two faces, the axis joining them is the axis of the loop, and the dipole is therefore placed ALONG the loop's axis.
(ii) THE MAGNETIC DIPOLE MOMENT.
Experiment and the field expressions both show the strength of the equivalent dipole to be proportional to the current and to the area enclosed:
\(M \propto I \qquad M \propto A\)
so for a single turn
\(\vec{M} = I\vec{A}\)
and for a coil of N turns, \(\vec{M} = NI\vec{A}\). Its SI unit is \(\mathrm{A\,m^{2}}\).
DIRECTION. \(\vec{M}\) is along the AREA VECTOR, that is PERPENDICULAR to the plane of the loop, its sense given by the right-hand rule: curl the fingers along the current and the thumb points along \(\vec{M}\).
(iii) THE COIL IN A UNIFORM EXTERNAL FIELD.
NET FORCE. The net force is ZERO. In a UNIFORM field the forces on opposite arms of the loop are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so they cancel; what remains is a COUPLE, which turns the coil without translating it. (A net force appears only in a non-uniform field.)
ORIENTATION OF STABLE EQUILIBRIUM. The potential energy of the coil is
\(U = -\vec{M} \cdot \vec{B} = -MB\cos\theta\)
which is least when \(\cos\theta = 1\), that is \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\). So stable equilibrium is the orientation in which \(\vec{M}\) is PARALLEL to \(\vec{B}\) — the plane of the coil perpendicular to the field. The torque \(\tau = MB\sin\theta\) is zero there, and any small displacement produces a torque restoring it.
WHY THE FLUX IS THEN MAXIMUM. In this orientation the area vector \(\vec{A}\) lies along \(\vec{B}\). The coil's OWN field, inside the coil, is along \(\vec{M}\) and hence also along \(\vec{B}\), so the two fields ADD rather than partly cancel. The flux of the total field through the coil is therefore
\(\phi = \left(B_{coil} + B_{ext}\right)A\)
with both terms positive and \(\cos\theta = 1\), which is its greatest possible value.
The three answers form one picture: the coil feels no net pull, only a twist, and it twists until it has as much flux through it as it can get. That is the same rule a compass needle obeys, and it is the basis of the electric motor — which prevents the coil from resting there by reversing the current each half turn.

rows.stem:
(i) A thin pencil of length (f/4) is placed coinciding with the principal axis of a mirror of focal length f. The image of the pencil is real and enlarged, just touches the pencil. Calculate the magnification produced by the mirror.
(ii) A ray of light is incident on a refracting face AB of a prism ABC at an angle of \(45^\circ\). The ray emerges from face AC and the angle of deviation is \(15^\circ\). The angle of prism is \(30^\circ\). Show that the emergent ray is normal to the face AC from which it emerges out. Find the refraction index of the material of the prism.
rows.solution:
(i) MAGNIFICATION PRODUCED BY THE MIRROR.
The clue is "the image just TOUCHES the pencil". For a concave mirror the one point that images onto ITSELF is the centre of curvature C, at a distance 2f. So the pencil must have one end AT C, and since the image is real and enlarged the pencil lies between F and C — the region that gives a real, inverted, magnified image.
POSITIONS OF THE TWO ENDS. One end is at 2f. The pencil has length \(\dfrac{f}{4}\) and extends towards the mirror, so the other end is at
\(u = -\left(2f - \dfrac{f}{4}\right) = -\dfrac{7f}{4}\)
IMAGE OF THAT END. With \(f\) negative for a concave mirror, so \(f \to -f\):
\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{4}{7f} = -\dfrac{1}{f}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{4}{7f} = \dfrac{-7 + 4}{7f} = -\dfrac{3}{7f}\)
\(v = -\dfrac{7f}{3}\)
MAGNIFICATION:
\(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{7f}{3}\right)}{\left(-\dfrac{7f}{4}\right)} = -\dfrac{4}{3}\)
The magnification is \(-\dfrac{4}{3}\), the negative sign recording that the image is INVERTED, as every real image in a mirror is.
As a check on the geometry: the near end images at \(\dfrac{7f}{3} \approx 2{\cdot}33f\) and the far end at \(2f\), so the image runs from \(2f\) to \(2{\cdot}33f\) and has length \(\dfrac{f}{3}\). Against an object length of \(\dfrac{f}{4}\), that is a ratio of \(\dfrac{4}{3}\) — enlarged, and just touching the object at C, exactly as the stem describes.
(ii) THE PRISM.
Use the prism relation connecting the four angles:
\(i + e = A + \delta\)
Substituting \(i = 45^{\circ}\), \(A = 30^{\circ}\) and \(\delta = 15^{\circ}\):
\(45^{\circ} + e = 30^{\circ} + 15^{\circ} = 45^{\circ}\)
\(e = 0^{\circ}\)
An angle of emergence of zero means the emergent ray makes no angle with the NORMAL to face AC — that is, the emergent ray is PERPENDICULAR to the face AC, which is what was to be shown.
The internal geometry confirms it. Since \(r_{1} + r_{2} = A\) and \(e = 0\) forces \(r_{2} = 0\),
\(r_{1} = A = 30^{\circ}\)
and Snell's law at the first face then gives the refractive index:
\(n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r_{1}} = \dfrac{\sin 45^{\circ}}{\sin 30^{\circ}} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}\)
\(n = \sqrt{2}\)
A ray leaving normally is not a coincidence of the numbers but a recognisable situation: it means the ray inside the prism struck AC along its normal, so it passed out without bending, and the entire \(15^{\circ}\) of deviation was produced at the FIRST face alone.

rows.stem:
(i) Light consisting of two wavelengths 600 nm and 480 nm is used to obtain interference fringes in a double slit experiment. The screen is placed 1.0 m away from slits which are 1.0 nm apart.
(1) Calculate the distance of the third bright fringe on the screen from the central maximum for wavelength 600 nm.
(2) Find the least distance from the central maximum where the bright fringes due to both the wavelengths coincide.
(ii) (1) Draw the variation of intensity with angle of diffraction in single slit diffraction pattern. Write the expression for value of angle corresponding to zero intensity locations.
(2) In what way diffraction of light waves differs from diffraction of sound waves ?
rows.solution:
[PAPER DEFECT, worked as printed. The stem states the slit separation as "1.0 nm". That cannot be what was intended — a separation of 1 nm is far SMALLER than the 600 nm wavelength, and since \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{n\lambda}{d}\) would then need to be 600 for even the first maximum, no interference pattern exists at all under the printed geometry. The intended figure is plainly 1.0 mm. CBSE'S OWN MARKING SCHEME FOLLOWED THE MISPRINT THROUGH, reaching 1800 m and 2400 m, so those are the answers the derivation below gives, with the intended values noted alongside.]
(i) (1) THE THIRD BRIGHT FRINGE.
The distance of the \(n^{th}\) bright fringe from the central maximum is
\(x_{n} = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}\)
With \(n = 3\), \(\lambda = 600\ \mathrm{nm} = 600 \times 10^{-9}\) m, \(D = 1{\cdot}0\) m and \(d = 1{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{nm} = 1 \times 10^{-9}\) m as printed:
\(x_{3} = \dfrac{3 \times 600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1}{1 \times 10^{-9}}\)
\(x_{3} = 1800\ \mathrm{m}\)
(With the intended \(d = 1{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{mm}\) this becomes \(1{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{mm}\), which is the physically sensible fringe spacing.)
(2) THE LEAST DISTANCE AT WHICH THE TWO PATTERNS COINCIDE.
Two bright fringes coincide when they lie at the same distance from the centre:
\(\dfrac{n_{1}\lambda_{1}D}{d} = \dfrac{n_{2}\lambda_{2}D}{d} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n_{1}\lambda_{1} = n_{2}\lambda_{2}\)
\(n_{1} \times 600 = n_{2} \times 480\)
\(\dfrac{n_{1}}{n_{2}} = \dfrac{480}{600} = \dfrac{4}{5}\)
The SMALLEST whole numbers satisfying this are \(n_{1} = 4\) and \(n_{2} = 5\): the \(4^{th}\) bright fringe of 600 nm falls on the \(5^{th}\) bright fringe of 480 nm.
\(x = \dfrac{4 \times 600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1}{1 \times 10^{-9}} = 2400\ \mathrm{m}\)
and as a check via the other wavelength, \(\dfrac{5 \times 480 \times 10^{-9} \times 1}{1 \times 10^{-9}} = 2400\) m, the same point.
(With the intended \(d = 1{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{mm}\) this is \(2{\cdot}4\ \mathrm{mm}\).)
(ii) (1) THE SINGLE-SLIT DIFFRACTION PATTERN.
Plot intensity against the angle of diffraction. The curve has a tall, broad CENTRAL MAXIMUM at \(\theta = 0\), falling to zero on either side, flanked by much fainter SECONDARY MAXIMA between successive zeros. Two features must be right: the central maximum is TWICE as wide as any secondary one, and the first secondary maximum is only about 4% as intense as the central one.
ANGLE FOR ZERO INTENSITY. The minima occur where
\(\theta = \dfrac{n\lambda}{a} \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)
with a the slit width. (The value \(n = 0\) is excluded — it is the central MAXIMUM, not a zero.)
(2) DIFFRACTION OF LIGHT COMPARED WITH SOUND.
Diffraction is appreciable only when the wavelength is comparable to the size of the obstacle or aperture.
LIGHT has wavelengths of a few hundred nanometres, vastly smaller than doors, windows or anything else it meets in ordinary life, so its diffraction goes unnoticed and light appears to travel in straight lines.
SOUND has wavelengths from centimetres to metres, comparable to everyday obstacles, so it diffracts strongly — which is why one can hear round a corner but not see round it.
